Talking, even returning a greeting, is not fitting in prayer, which is glorification, takbir and recitation; a verse commanded silence, and the Prophet only gestured when greeted while praying.
A wicked jinn, in another report Iblis with a flame of fire, tried to disrupt the Prophet's prayer; he would have bound him but for his brother Solomon's supplication.
The Prophet led prayer carrying his granddaughter Umama, prayed on his new pulpit to teach the prayer, forbade hands on the waist, and allowed removing pebbles only once.
The Prophet scraped spittle off the qibla wall and told worshippers to spit only left, under the foot; spitting in the mosque is a sin, expiated by burying it.
Anas said the Prophet prayed in his shoes, and a garment with designs that distracted the Prophet in prayer he sent to Abu Jahm for a plain one.
When supper is served as the prayer begins, eat first rather than hurry to pray; Aisha cited the Prophet: no prayer is right with food present or when nature calls.
Whoever eats garlic, onion or leek should keep away from the mosque, for the smell harms angels and people, though the Prophet would not forbid what Allah made lawful.
One who hears a man calling out in the mosque for something lost should say, May Allah not restore it to you, for mosques were not built for this.
If the devil confuses a worshipper's count, or he misses the sitting after two rak'ahs as the Prophet did, he prostrates twice sitting, building on what he is sure of.
The Prophet, after praying five rak'ahs or adding or omitting something, made two prostrations, saying he forgot as others forget, and told the doubtful to aim at what is correct.
When the Prophet ended prayer after two or three rak'ahs, a long-armed man asked whether it was shortened or he had forgotten; he completed it and made two prostrations.
The Prophet and those with him prostrated on reciting verses of prostration, including al-Najm and 'When the heaven burst asunder', though once, when Zaid recited al-Najm, he did not.
Sitting for the tashahhud, the Prophet placed his hands on his thighs or knees and pointed with his forefinger, and ended the prayer with salutations to the right and left.
In the Prophet's time the end of the obligatory prayer was known by the takbir and the remembrance of Allah said aloud.
Jewish women told Aisha of torment in the grave; after a revelation the Prophet confirmed that the dead are tried in their graves and sought refuge from it in prayer.
In prayer, after the tashahhud, the Prophet sought and taught refuge from the torment of Hell and the grave, the trial of life and death, the Dajjal, sin and debt.
After the salutation the Prophet asked forgiveness thrice, said 'Thou art Peace', and affirmed there is no god but Allah alone, none withholding what He gives; Ibn Zubair said likewise.
The Prophet taught the poor emigrants to glorify, praise and magnify Allah thirty-three times each after every prayer; the wealthy copied it, and sins abundant as sea foam are forgiven.
Between the opening takbir and the recitation the Prophet silently asked Allah to remove and wash away his sins, but in the second rak'ah he began al-Fatiha without pause.
Two men said words of praise in prayer; the Prophet said twelve angels vied to take one man's words up and heaven's doors opened for the other's.
When the iqama is said, come to prayer walking calmly, not running, pray what you catch with the imam and complete what you missed.
At the iqama people were not to stand till they saw the Prophet; once he left the formed rows to bathe, and Bilal said the iqama only on seeing him.
Whoever catches one rak'ah of the prayer, with the imam in one wording, has caught the prayer.
Whoever catches one rak'ah of the dawn prayer before sunrise, or of the afternoon prayer before sunset, has caught that prayer.
When Umar b. Abd al-Aziz delayed prayer, Urwa reported Gabriel leading the Prophet in the five prayers, and Aisha his afternoon prayer while sunlight was in her room.
The Prophet set the limits of each prayer's time, and showed an inquirer by praying early one day and late the next, saying the time lies between.
The noon prayer is delayed in intense heat till it cools, for such heat is Hell's exhalation; the Fire, complaining, was allowed two breaths, in winter and summer.
The Prophet prayed noon once the sun declined and did not respond to complaints about praying on scorching ground; in the heat some prostrated on their spread cloth.
The afternoon prayer was prayed early enough to reach Quba or cook and eat a camel before sunset; the hypocrite waits till the sun is between the devil's horns.
Whoever misses the afternoon prayer is as though he has been deprived of his family and his property.
At Ahzab the enemy kept the Prophet from the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer, till sunset, and he asked Allah to fill their houses and graves with fire.
Aisha had her copy of the Quran written 'Guard the prayers and the middle prayer and the afternoon prayer', saying she heard it so from the Prophet.
At the Ditch Umar and the Prophet had both missed the afternoon prayer; the Prophet made ablution, prayed it after sunset, then prayed the evening prayer.
Angels gather at the dawn and afternoon prayers; believers will see their Lord as they see the moon, and whoever keeps these two prayers will enter Paradise, not the Fire.
The Prophet prayed the evening prayer as soon as the sun had set, and afterwards one could still see where his arrow fell.
The Prophet once delayed the night prayer till many slept, saying no others waited for it and he would pray then were it not a burden on his community.
The Prophet sometimes delayed Isha until people slept or near midnight, said those waiting were in prayer, and would have ordered that hour were it not hard on his Ummah.
The Prophet told people not to let the bedouins prevail over the name of their night prayer, which is Isha in the Book of Allah, though bedouins call it Atama.
Believing women prayed the morning prayer with the Prophet and went home wrapped in their mantles, unrecognisable in the darkness before dawn.
Jabir and Abu Barza described the Prophet's prayer times, from noon in the midday heat to dawn in early darkness; he disliked sleeping before Isha and talking after it.
